doc.title: Jerry Jerome interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

title: Segregation in Kansas City and Alabama
summary: The club was not segregated but Kansas City was; he recalls being thrown out of an Earl Hines show in Alabama in 1933-34.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was the atmosphere, was it semi-segregated?
It was totally segregated. How did you fit into that?
Well. You are talking about the place?
No, no the place was not segregated at all. But the feeling in Kansas City was. Blacks were blacks and whites were whites. That’s the way it was.
But you were accepted because you were a player?
Yeah. And no one bothered me. When I went to the University of Alabama and I went to hear Earl Hines, they kicked me out. They says you ain’t got no business being here, get out. Cops.

Uh, ‘33 — ‘34. And this wasn’t that much different in Kansas City I don’t think, but I never saw any blacks in any good jobs or anything like that. I think they were segregated at that point. But I went anyway. And if they gave me a bad time I’d get out. I never would fight cops or do anything like that, but I liked to go where I liked to go. And so I sat in with Basie a few times, and it was just fabulous. I was just absorbing him, and what I was hearing out of Lester Young, he was just incredible. And a very quiet man too. He was to himself. But I of course took up with the Basie band when they came to New York when I heard the big band. But that turned my thing around. I said this is the way to play a horn. Because you know coming out of the twenties you heard Paul Whiteman, Bert Lown, and even Casa Loma — it was a good band but it was not a jazz band, the players was not —
